_notes.usage: Copy this file to config.json and fill in real values. config.json is gitignored-by-convention and should never be committed (it holds credentials).
_notes.model_path / paddleocr model dirs: model_path (the YOLO weights, e.g. best.pt) and alpr.paddleocr_det_model_dir/paddleocr_rec_model_dir/paddleocr_cls_model_dir are all resolved relative to the FOLDER config.json ACTUALLY LOADED FROM, not the code's location -- so by default everything lives together in one folder. det and rec are REAL, required models -- place the actual downloaded files there (flat, no subfolders: inference.pdmodel/inference.pdiparams/inference.pdiparams.info). cls (angle classifier) is different: PaddleOCR's constructor unconditionally tries to download it regardless of use_angle_cls, but the code always passes use_angle_cls=false, and confirmed from paddleocr's own source, the classifier object that would actually READ those files is only ever instantiated when use_angle_cls=true -- so cls's file CONTENT never matters, only its existence. The service creates empty placeholder files there itself on first run (see worker.py's ensure_cls_placeholder) specifically so a machine with no route to paddleocr.bj.bcebos.com -- e.g. behind a corporate proxy blocking that download's HTTPS tunnel, a real failure this was written to fix -- never needs a real cls model at all. You never need to place cls files yourself; if you see it trying to download anyway, delete any partial/leftover file in paddleocr_models/cls first, then restart.
_notes.mqtt.trigger_enabled / http_trigger: Two independent, combinable trigger sources. mqtt.trigger_enabled (default true) subscribes to the VCA event topics below as before. http_trigger.enabled (default false) instead/additionally runs an HTTP server (served by waitress, a production WSGI server -- not Flask's dev server) that a camera's own alarm task (e.g. a Bosch dome's built-in 'HTTP notification' action) calls directly on a rule trigger, bypassing Genetec/MQTT for the trigger itself. MQTT stays connected and is always used to publish results either way -- disabling mqtt.trigger_enabled only stops it from subscribing. At least one of the two must be enabled. See the 'http_trigger' block below for its own settings.
_notes.http_trigger.port/threads: port must match whatever the camera's Alarm Task Editor HttpCommand is configured to send to (its Port(...) value) -- a mismatch means the request never arrives. threads is waitress's worker pool size; the default of 4 is plenty for this endpoint's workload (a handful of alarm hits per truck, each just a dict lookup + queue put). GET /healthz always returns 200 if the server is up, independent of ALPR's own health, for a process supervisor/load balancer to poll.
_notes.http_trigger SSL: If the camera's HttpCommand has SSL(false) (the default in Bosch's Alarm Task Editor), plain HTTP is all that's needed -- nothing else to configure. Only if a camera is set to SSL(true) would this need a certificate (e.g. a self-signed cert passed to waitress, or a reverse proxy terminating TLS in front of it) -- not set up here since it isn't needed for SSL(false).
_notes.snapshot: Every camera is pulled via a single HTTP GET to its snapshot endpoint (e.g. a Bosch dome's /snap.jpg), authenticated with HTTP Digest, using one common username/password for ALL cameras -- there's no per-camera override and no RTSP/Genetec path anymore (removed in favor of this). During a collection window the service polls this endpoint repeatedly (as fast as the HTTP round trip allows, or paced by poll_interval_ms) instead of decoding a continuous video stream. Chosen because trigger events here are trucks crawling in slowly, not fast drive-bys, so RTSP's much higher frame rate wasn't needed to catch a good shot.
_notes.snapshot.url_template: Default matches a Bosch FLEXIDOME 3000i/5000i's snapshot path: http://ip:80/snap.jpg. Confirm on your specific unit's web UI under RTSP/streaming (or HTTP) settings if snapshots fail or come back low-res.
_notes.alpr.expected_frame_width/height: Set to your camera's real sensor resolution (e.g. a 5MP camera is commonly 2592x1944) to catch the snapshot endpoint unexpectedly serving a lower-res image than the camera's actual sensor. Leave both null to disable the check.
_notes.logging.level: Text log verbosity: DEBUG / INFO / WARNING / ERROR. Independent of alpr.diagnostics_mode below, but diagnostics_mode='troubleshooting' forces this to DEBUG regardless of what's set here.
_notes.alpr.diagnostics_mode: 'basic' (default): saves the first fetched frame + its ROI crop, the OCR-attempted crops, and the OCR-prep images -- fine for normal operation. 'troubleshooting': all of that PLUS every fetched frame (full image and ROI), the ROI annotated with every box the model returned (green=kept, red=rejected-by-size/position, orange=rejected-as-duplicate, with the rejection reason labeled), and every kept candidate crop saved the instant it's found, not just the ones that got OCR'd -- and forces logging to DEBUG. Use this to see WHY, e.g., ocr_attempts stays at 0 (wrong ROI vs. camera framing? model detecting nothing at all vs. detecting boxes but all getting filtered out?). Generates a lot more files per event -- meant to be turned on temporarily while diagnosing, then switched back to 'basic'.
_notes.alpr.max_ocr_attempts / collection_timeo: The first detected plate box in ANY frame is the trigger to start OCRing immediately -- best-scoring candidate first within a frame, continuing across subsequent frames -- and the whole collection stops the instant one produces a plate that passes plate_text.is_valid(), rather than waiting out the full collection window and voting across whatever showed up. max_ocr_attempts caps how many OCR calls one collection window will make (across all frames, not per frame) before giving up; collection_timeout is a wall-clock backstop on top of that (e.g. a truck that never presents a readable plate). There is no fallback vote if the budget runs out with nothing valid -- the result is NO_VALID_PLATE, and every individual attempt (valid or not) is still in the audit result.json's 'reads' array for forensics. A near-duplicate crop (the same plate, barely moved between two consecutive frames) does not consume a fresh attempt -- it's skipped before OCR runs, same duplicate_diff_threshold/duplicate_resize_* comparison as before.
_notes.alpr.upper_half_fraction: A detected box is rejected as 'upper_half' if its vertical center sits above this fraction of the ROI's height (0.45 = reject anything in the top 45%). Meant to filter false positives from cab signage/mounting hardware above the real plate -- but if your camera's mounting angle puts the real plate legitimately high in the ROI, this will silently discard correct detections (confirmed via diagnostics_mode='troubleshooting': the model boxed the plate correctly but it was labeled upper_half). Lower it (e.g. 0.15) or set to 0 to disable the check entirely if that happens.
_notes.alpr.plate_crop_padding_pct: Expands each detected box by this percent of its own width/height (each side) before cropping for OCR, clamped to the ROI's bounds. Fixes a real observed failure: a slightly undersized YOLO box clips a character off the plate's edge -- confirmed via two adjacent, overlapping detections that each only captured half a plate ('HR47E' / 'E4812', sharing the boundary 'E', for what was actually 'HR47E4812'). Set to 0 to disable; raise it if plates are still getting clipped, lower it if crops start including too much surrounding clutter.
_notes.event_filter: Trigger events carry a VCA classification per detected object, e.g. Data.Object.Object.Appearance.Class.Type = {"#text": "Vehicle", "@Likelihood": 0.91}. Only events with a detection matching one of class_types (case-insensitive) at or above min_likelihood are queued for ALPR -- everything else (Person/Bicycle detections, low-confidence hits, events with no classified object) is discarded before a single snapshot is fetched. Tune min_likelihood against the values your camera actually reports (0.91 in the sample payload this was built from).
_notes.event_filter.class_types (disabling): Set class_types to an empty array, [], to disable this filter entirely and queue EVERY line-crossing event regardless of classification -- min_likelihood is then ignored too. Do not just delete min_likelihood or set it to 0/null while leaving class_types non-empty -- the event still has to match one of class_types first, so that alone would not stop filtering.
_notes.alpr.publish_no_valid_plate: true (default): every trigger gets an MQTT reply regardless of read success -- a NO_VALID_PLATE collection still publishes {..., "truck_number": "UNKNOWN", "status": "NO_VALID_PLATE", ...} so a downstream consumer knows the event was processed, not just silence. (truck_number is never null -- see alpr.unknown_plate_value.) The audit folder (result.json/event.json) is always written either way. Camera/system errors (CAMERA_UNREACHABLE, CAMERA_CONFIG_ERROR, FRAME_SIZE_ERROR, ERROR) are unaffected and always publish regardless of this setting. Set false to only publish actual successful reads -- note that doing so also means a no-read visit produces no message at all, which is the one case where "always reports a truck number" stops applying.
_notes.mqtt enter/leave (filtering): Entering and leaving are two independent triggers, each its own MQTT subscription -- which rule/event types reach this service at all is decided by these topic filters (MQTT wildcards), not by any code-side filtering. Confirmed against real captured events for the SAME tracked object (ObjectId) a few seconds apart: enter_subscribe_topic matches 'Camera_Events/AR-H6/onvif-ej/RuleEngine/LineDetector/Crossed/&1/Entering field 2' (event_type=LineDetector; this same topic shape also covers plain 'Crossing line N' rules), and leave_subscribe_topic matches 'Camera_Events/AR-H6/onvif-ej/RuleEngine/ObjectTrack/Aggregation/&1/Leaving field 3' (event_type=ObjectTrack) -- '+' matches exactly one topic segment, '#' matches all remaining segments (only valid at the end, absorbs the varying '&1/<free text>' suffix). The two are structurally distinct (LineDetector/Crossed vs ObjectTrack/Aggregation) so there's no overlap between them.
_notes.mqtt enter/leave (results): Each direction publishes to its own topic (enter_result_topic_prefix/<bay> or leave_result_topic_prefix/<bay>) with a lean payload -- bay, direction, truck_number, confidence, status, event_time/ocr_time -- so a downstream gate/dock system can subscribe to entries and exits separately without parsing the fuller record. The complete detail (every OCR read, collection stats, rejection reasons) is still written to the audit folder's result.json regardless.
_notes.mqtt.bay_segment_index: 0-based position of the bay name within the subscribe topics, e.g. 1 for 'Camera_Events/<bay>/...'. Shared by both enter and leave since they use the same layout; adjust if yours differs.
_notes.bay_monitor: A separate, optional feature from the enter/leave ALPR pipeline above -- off by default (enabled: false). Continuously round-robins every enabled camera (independent of MQTT/HTTP triggers) looking for presence via a plain frame-diff against the ROI's last-seen-empty state -- deliberately NOT the ALPR plate model, since a bay is occupied or not regardless of whether a plate happens to be visible (a reversed-in trailer's plate usually faces away from the dock camera entirely). Once a bay's scene changes it's 'zoomed in': every classify_interval_sec (default 60s) a frame is sent to a local Ollama-hosted vision model and the reply (one of status_values) is published to mqtt.bay_status_topic_prefix + '/<bay>'. After empty_debounce_count consecutive 'empty' replies it reverts to baseline scanning. ollama_model has NO working default -- it must be set to a vision-capable model tag you've actually pulled locally (`ollama pull <tag>`), and the service fails fast at startup if enabled without one set, rather than silently misclassifying everything.
_notes.bay_monitor.baseline_scan_interval_ms: Pacing between each camera checked in the round-robin (applies whether or not anything was found) -- keeps the scanner from hammering every camera back-to-back with zero gap. Does not apply to the classify_interval_sec cadence of a zoomed-in bay's LLM calls, which is separately paced.
_notes.bay_monitor.reference_images: Optional few-shot exemplars sent alongside every classification call, e.g. [{"path": "reference_images/empty.jpg", "label": "empty"}, {"path": "reference_images/door_open.jpg", "label": "occupied (bay door open)"}]. Paths resolve relative to config.json's directory, like model_path. Loaded once at startup, not re-read per call -- a missing file is logged and skipped, not fatal. Helps most on real ambiguous cases a text-only prompt undersells, e.g. an open bay/cargo door that can otherwise get misread as empty or throw off the model.
_notes.bay_state_engine: Off by default; depends entirely on bay_monitor also being enabled (fails startup otherwise). When on, it becomes the authority for enter/leave direction and timing INSTEAD of the MQTT/HTTP trigger source: bay_monitor's own empty->occupied transition enqueues an ALPR read via the normal Worker pool, and (unlike a one-shot trigger) keeps retrying every time bay_monitor reclassifies the bay as still occupied, until a read actually succeeds -- so a bad read caused by e.g. a bay/cargo door being open doesn't cost the whole visit's identity, just that one attempt. occupied->empty then publishes the leave result using whatever plate got confirmed at ANY point during the stay (there's no fresh camera read at that instant to attempt, since 'empty' means the truck's no longer in frame). If mqtt.trigger_enabled or http_trigger.enabled are ALSO on at the same time, both paths independently decide enter/leave for the same bays -- a startup warning (not a hard failure) flags this, since it usually means redundant or conflicting publishes; turn the old trigger(s) off if bay_state_engine is meant to be the sole source of truth. State is in-memory only -- a restart loses any truck currently mid-visit.
_notes.mqtt.bay_state_topic_prefix: Where bay_state_engine publishes its LIVE per-bay session ('/<bay>' appended) -- {bay, open, direction, plate, confidence, read_attempts, timestamp} -- on every state change: arrival (session opens), a plate getting confirmed, and departure (session closes). This is separate from, and unconditional unlike, mqtt.enter_result_topic_prefix/leave_result_topic_prefix -- those only ever fire once per visit (on departure) and are suppressed entirely by alpr.publish_no_valid_plate=false when nothing was confirmed; this topic always fires regardless, since its purpose is showing the engine is alive and reacting, not delivering a final result to a downstream gate/dock system. Only published if bay_state_engine.enabled is true.
_notes.thresholds (all in config now): Every numeric decision boundary the code makes is a config value with no separate code-level default of its own beyond what's documented here -- nothing requires a code change to retune. alpr.yolo_conf_threshold is the minimum YOLO box confidence for a plate detection to be considered at all (Ultralytics' own unstated default is 0.25 if not set). bay_monitor's own baseline presence check is unrelated to this model or threshold -- see bay_monitor.presence_diff_* below. alpr.score_weights (plus score_area_norm/score_sharpness_norm) control how multiple candidate crops from one collection window get ranked against each other; alpr.duplicate_resize_width/_height/duplicate_diff_threshold control when two crops are treated as the same sighting rather than voted on twice; alpr.ocr_prep_target_height/ocr_prep_padding control how a crop is resized/bordered before OCR; alpr.max_consecutive_fetch_failures/fetch_failure_backoff_sec control when a collection window gives up on a camera that's not responding.
_notes.alpr.unknown_plate_value: Every published result carries a truck_number STRING, never null -- anything short of a valid read reports this placeholder ('UNKNOWN' by default) instead, so a downstream consumer never has to null-check the field. The 'status' field (SUCCESS / NO_VALID_PLATE / CAMERA_UNREACHABLE / CAMERA_CONFIG_ERROR / FRAME_SIZE_ERROR / ERROR) is what distinguishes a genuine read from the placeholder. Keep it to something no real plate could be -- it must not satisfy the Indian-plate patterns in plate_text.py, or a placeholder could be mistaken for a real read. Note this is about the VALUE reported; alpr.publish_no_valid_plate separately controls whether a no-read result is published at all (leave it true if you want an update on every trigger regardless of outcome). The audit result.json additionally keeps 'final_plate' (same value as truck_number on SUCCESS, null otherwise) and the full 'reads' array -- every individual OCR attempt, valid or not -- so the placeholder never hides forensic detail.
_notes.bay_monitor.empty_status / classify_regi: empty_status names which entry of status_values means 'nothing is there'; it drives both bay_monitor's revert-to-baseline debounce and bay_state_engine's occupied set (everything that isn't it), so a custom status_values vocabulary works end to end without either hardcoding the literal 'empty'. classify_region picks which pixels the vision model judges: 'full_frame' (default) shows it the whole bay -- cargo, forklifts, doors, which is what the activity vocabulary is really about -- but a truck in an ADJACENT bay that's also in shot can then drive this bay's status (and, with bay_state_engine on, open a session on the wrong bay). Set it to 'roi' to restrict classification to the same cameras.json roi presence detection uses, removing that cross-talk at the cost of a much narrower view (the roi is framed for plates, not for watching cargo movement). Use 'roi' if your bays overlap in frame.
_notes.service.num_workers/queue_max: num_workers is roughly 'how many trucks this instance can process at once' -- each Worker thread owns its own loaded YOLO+PaddleOCR models (~2GB RAM apiece), so this is a memory/CPU sizing knob, not just a throughput one. queue_max caps how many pending jobs JobBus holds before it starts dropping new ones instead of growing unbounded.
_notes.alpr.max_read_attempts: Ceiling on how many ALPR reads bay_state_engine queues for one visit while the plate is still unconfirmed. The truck is stationary and the camera fixed, so attempt N photographs the same obscured plate attempt 1 did; left uncapped, a truck parked for hours with an unreadable plate re-runs a full collection every cooldown window indefinitely, each one holding one of only service.num_workers threads and starving genuinely new arrivals. Only consulted by bay_state_engine -- the MQTT/HTTP trigger paths are one-shot and unaffected.
_notes.alpr.model_load_max_retries / model_load: Each Worker thread retries loading YOLO+PaddleOCR this many times (backoff_sec apart) before giving up -- a transient failure (a network blip fetching a model file, a proxy hiccup) shouldn't need a full process restart to recover from. If every attempt still fails, that worker thread does NOT die silently the way it used to (an uncaught exception in a background thread just prints a traceback and vanishes, with nothing published anywhere and jobs left to queue forever) -- it stays alive and publishes a MODEL_LOAD_FAILED error result for every job it's handed instead, so a downstream consumer gets a signal and the cause is visible on the result topic, not just buried in a log file nobody's watching.
_notes.bay_monitor.classify_max_dimension / cla: classify_max_dimension downscales a frame so its longest side is at most this many pixels before it is JPEG-encoded and sent to the vision model (0 disables downscaling). This matters more than it looks: a vision model's prefill cost scales with pixel count, and a raw 5MP snapshot is ~6x the pixels of a 1024-wide view -- on a CPU-only box that difference routinely exceeds ollama_timeout_sec, and a timeout discards the fetch, the encode and the partial inference alike, leaving the bay with no status at all. Reference exemplars are downscaled the same way, once at startup, so they don't multiply the per-call bill.
_notes.bay_monitor.presence_diff_*: The entire baseline presence check: a small thumbnail of the ROI is compared against the one from the last time this bay was looked at while empty -- deliberately NOT the ALPR plate model (a bay is occupied or not regardless of whether a plate happens to be visible in frame). A resize+diff (~100us) is the whole cost, run every baseline_scan_interval_ms round. A change big enough to matter -- a truck arriving -- moves far more pixels than presence_diff_threshold tolerates, so this cannot miss an arrival. The cached thumbnail is cleared on both the arrival and departure transitions, so it never compares against a frame from before/after a visit. Set presence_diff_enabled to false to report presence unconditionally on every round instead (bypasses the check entirely -- useful for tuning classify_interval_sec/the prompt without waiting for an actual scene change).
_notes.bay_monitor.classify_diff_*: The same thumbnail-diff mechanism as presence_diff_*, but answering a different question: once a bay is already zoomed in, has the scene changed enough since the last classify to reclassify right now (e.g. idle -> unloading) instead of waiting out classify_interval_sec? Runs ALONGSIDE that timer, not instead of it, so a zoomed-in bay is now fetched every baseline_scan_interval_ms round (not just when the timer is due) -- a subtle change too small to trip classify_diff_threshold still gets caught on the next scheduled tick either way. Uses its own threshold, separate from presence_diff_threshold, since 'is anything here at all' and 'did an established truck's activity change' don't need the same sensitivity. Set classify_diff_enabled to false to go back to pure timer-only reclassification.
_notes.bay_monitor.ollama_think: Sent as the /api/generate 'think' field. Reasoning models (e.g. qwen3) emit a hidden 'thinking' trace before their actual answer unless told not to -- confirmed on a real deployment to cut one classify call from ~31.7s to ~6.4s once set to false. Safe to leave false even for non-reasoning models, which just ignore a field they don't recognize.
_notes.bay_monitor.save_latest_frame: Overwrites audit/<bay>/latest_frame.jpg on every successful snapshot fetch -- a live 'what does this camera see right now' view for remote troubleshooting (confirming framing/focus/ROI without direct access to the camera feed), without the volume of diagnostics_mode='troubleshooting''s per-event dumps. One file per bay, always the most recent, never accumulates.
_notes.alpr.save_detected_plate_frames: On every SUCCESS result, copies the crop that actually produced the winning plate into a separate, flat audit/detected_plates/ folder (named '<timestamp>_<bay>_<direction>_<plate>.jpg') -- so confirmed reads can be browsed chronologically at a glance across all bays, without hunting through each job's own per-event audit subfolder. The full per-job detail (result.json, every candidate crop) is still written to its usual per-event folder either way.

bay_monitor.classification_prompt: You are monitoring a truck loading dock bay through a fixed security camera. Classify the current activity into EXACTLY ONE of these words: empty, occupied, unloading, loading, idle. 'empty' = no truck present. 'occupied' = a truck is present but no cargo movement is visible. 'unloading' = cargo is visibly being removed from the truck. 'loading' = cargo is visibly being loaded onto the truck. 'idle' = a truck is present, not actively loading or unloading (e.g. waiting, doors closed, driver break). Respond with only the single classification word, nothing else.
